metadata.description: The Open-Source Gateway to Your Digital Publishing Utopia.
metadata.title: {name} — The Open-Source Gateway to Your Digital Publishing Utopia

hero.title: The open-source gateway to your digital publishing utopia.
hero.lead: Publira is a multi-tenant SaaS that gives publishers with limited IT resources a digital distribution platform for manga and novels, run under their own brand. Editors submit the book information they receive from creators, and readers read it on the web or on mobile.

status.title: Still being built
status.body: Publira is under active development and has not reached a stable release. Everything shown on this page runs today, and an install can be brought up from its images with one Compose file, but running it for a real publisher still means reading the code, adapting it to your own environment, and following changes that are still landing. Take it as something to evaluate, build on, and contribute to — not as a finished product.

screenshot.caption: The catalog of a tenant site, running on the development seed data.

projects.title: One platform, and the two libraries it grew
projects.lead: Publira is the platform. Two of the pieces it needed grew into libraries of their own, and both are published for anyone to use without the rest of it.

publira.description: The platform itself: three Next.js apps, a Go server and worker that run from one image, a Flutter mobile client, and the Compose stack that runs them all locally.

comicViewer.description: The React comic viewer behind the episode screen. Headless by design, so the surrounding product supplies every pixel of the UI and the data pipeline.

epub.description: A Go library for decoding, encoding, and validating EPUB 3, built around io.ReaderAt so a publication never has to touch the filesystem.

platform.title: What a publisher gets on day one
platform.lead: A publisher gets a reader-facing site, an app, an editorial console, and — for whoever runs the install — a console above them all.

multiTenant.title: Multi-tenant from the ground up
multiTenant.body: Every publisher runs under its own brand and domain. Above them, the platform console — or publiractl, for an install that runs without it — manages tenant status, the operators, the readers of every tenant, and the settings the whole install shares: object storage, mail, Web Push, and security policy.

console.title: One console for the whole catalog
console.body: Series, episodes, labels, authors and the roles they are credited in, genres, tags, pages, announcements, access tickets, comments, and the messages readers send through the contact form, all from one console with a queue of everything awaiting release. A tenant admin invites the rest of the staff from it too.

themes.title: Themes with a real preview
themes.body: Colors, typefaces, logo, and icon are edited against a live preview built from the same parts as the public site, and the site keeps its current theme until this one is saved.

payments.title: Paid episodes, through the provider you choose
payments.body: A tenant sells episodes through Stripe or PAY.JP Checkout on the web, and through the App Store and Google Play in its app. The redirect unlocks nothing: a purchase is written when the provider's signed notification arrives, and a refund is recorded against the purchase it reverses.

signIn.title: Sign in with Apple and Google
signIn.body: Each tenant registers its own Apple and Google credentials, and its readers sign in with them on the site and in the app as well as with an email address. Tenant staff can turn on two-step verification, and the platform can require it of every tenant administrator.

surfaces.title: The site, the app, or both
surfaces.body: A series can be kept to the site or to the app, and an episode can narrow it further; the server answers every catalog read for the surface that asks. Where an episode is sold is set the same way, from a tenant default down to the episode itself.

royalties.title: Royalties, closed month by month
royalties.body: Each credited author carries a share of an episode's sales. A month closes into a statement — by hand, or on the day the tenant chooses — and a closed statement downloads as CSV. An author linked to a reader account reads their own episodes without buying them, and cannot rate them.

ageRatings.title: Age ratings under the tenant's own rule
ageRatings.body: R15 and R18 titles are marked wherever they are listed, hidden until the reader confirms, gated on the birth date the account carries under the verification rule each tenant chooses, and ranked in charts of their own that only a reader who may see them can open.

comments.title: Comments, and the queue behind them
comments.body: Readers comment where an episode ends, under the mode its series publishes in. Staff work through what was posted and what was flagged, and a withdrawn comment is purged once its retention window has passed.

engagement.title: What readers do feeds the catalog
engagement.body: Follows, reactions, and read-through are recorded per episode, rated into a score for the series, and aggregated into the daily and weekly charts by a batch job.

notifications.title: Notifications wherever the reader is
notifications.body: A new episode reaches a follower in the reader's inbox, as mail the worker delivers, as a Web Push notification the browser shows once the reader has allowed it, and as a push notification on the phone that opens the episode in the app.

mail.title: Mail that reads well
mail.body: Account mail — confirming an address, resetting a password, a changed address — and the contact form's notice to staff are drawn from React components into HTML under the tenant's name and in its language, with a plain-text part beside it. The renderer is an optional service of its own; without it the same mail goes out as plain text.

auditLog.title: An audit log per tenant
auditLog.body: Who did what, when, and how it turned out — filtered by period, action, or actor, with dates read as calendar days in the tenant's own time zone.

databaseRoles.title: Role-separated database access
databaseRoles.body: The reader-facing API, the tenant console, the platform console, and each background job connect to PostgreSQL as roles of their own, with row-level security keeping every tenant's rows apart, so the reader-facing site cannot reach what only an operator should see.

storage.title: Object storage and image delivery
storage.body: Episode pages, eye-catches, and genre artwork upload to the S3-compatible bucket the install is set up with, and the server resizes and converts them to WebP or AVIF on the way out, taking the same path locally as it does in production.

cache.title: A cache built for many instances
cache.body: "use cache", ISR, route handlers, fetch, and the next/image results are all shared through Redis, so a deployment can run more than one instance.

offline.title: Built for a dropped connection
offline.body: When the connection drops, a navigation, a prefetch, or a form submission waits for it to return instead of failing, and every screen of the three web apps says the connection is gone rather than looking like a slow server.

localization.title: Localized end to end
localization.body: English, Japanese, Korean, and Chinese in both scripts, on the reader site, in both consoles, in the app, and in the mail. A tenant's own pages — its terms and its privacy policy among them — carry a translation per language, and its time zone governs how its records are read.

searchEngines.title: Found by search engines
searchEngines.body: Every tenant site serves its own robots.txt and sitemap, and every public page names its canonical address and the same page in each of the other languages, so a search engine indexes each publisher as the site it is.

mobile.title: A reader app in the same repository
mobile.body: A Flutter client for Android and iOS under the tenant's own name and theme, calling the same public API as the site: accounts from sign-up to deletion, Sign in with Apple and Google, search, genres and tags, follows, an inbox, purchases in the store or through the site's checkout, and episodes saved encrypted on the device to read with no network. Each tenant builds its own app from one manifest.

portability.title: Yours to run anywhere
portability.body: Apache-2.0, an image for every process, one Compose file that runs an install on a single host, and publiractl to migrate the database and set the install up. Ordinary infrastructure underneath and no managed service in the way — portability and freedom from lock-in are the point, not a side effect.

screens.title: Four surfaces, one catalog
screens.lead: Three Next.js apps, a Flutter client, and the mail they send, each with its own audience. Every screenshot below is the development seed data, and the scenario seeds, that ship with the repository.

host.title: The reader-facing site
host.description: The site a reader lands on, published under the publisher's own brand. Browsing, searching, ranking, following, signing in, and the viewer that turns the pages.

admin.title: The tenant console
admin.description: Where editors work: the catalog and the publishing queue, the payment and sign-in providers, the theme and the pages of the public site, the messages readers send, what each author is owed, and the record of every change made to any of it.

platform.title: The platform console
platform.description: One level above the tenants, for whoever operates the install: what the install still needs set up, tenant status, cross-tenant events, the readers of every tenant, and the settings every tenant shares, from object storage to security policy.

mobile.title: The mobile app
mobile.description: The same catalog on a phone, from one Flutter codebase for Android and iOS, under the tenant's own name and theme. It calls the public API directly rather than going through the site, signs a reader in with an email address, Apple, or Google, sells episodes through the store or the site's checkout, and keeps the episodes a reader has opened or saved on the device.

mail.title: The mail it sends
mail.description: Account mail and the notices staff receive, drawn as HTML from React components by a renderer of its own and sent with a plain-text part beside it. Mail to a tenant's readers and staff carries the tenant's name rather than Publira's and is written in the tenant's language; in Japanese, Korean, and Chinese the spacing between scripts is left to the mail client's text rendering, as it is on the site.

dialog.open: Open the {title} screenshot of {address} at full size
dialog.openView: Open {view}, a screenshot of {title} on {address}, at full size

catalog.title: Catalog
catalog.caption: The work the tenant is leading with, above the shelves the rest of the page is built from: the week's chart, the newest episodes, the day's schedule, and the labels and authors it wants read. An announcement the console pins runs across the top of every page until the reader closes it, and everything carries the publisher's brand rather than Publira's.

browse.title: Genres
browse.caption: Each genre drawn from the covers of the series it ranks highest, or from artwork the editors upload for it, with the number of series behind it. A genre opens into its series, sorted and narrowed the way the whole list is, and the genres themselves are the tenant's own classification rather than a fixed list.

ranking.title: Ranking
ranking.caption: The daily chart and the weekly one, each row carrying how far the series moved since the chart before it. The positions come from what readers did — episodes opened and reacted to — aggregated by a batch job rather than arranged by hand, and R15 and R18 titles are ranked in charts of their own that open only to a reader who may see them.

seriesList.title: Series
seriesList.caption: Every published series, sorted and narrowed by genre, by serialization status, or down to the ones with free episodes. An age-rated title is marked wherever it is listed and stays hidden until the reader has confirmed they can see it.

seriesDetail.title: Series detail
seriesDetail.caption: The cover, synopsis, label, genres, and tags, with every author in the role they are credited in, and Follow and Share beside them. The episodes run below in reading order, each marked free or paid, so what can be read now is clear before anyone signs in.

viewer.title: Episode viewer
viewer.caption: Pages drawn on a canvas and turned as spreads, right to left, from the page the editor set the spreads to start on. The toolbar's slider moves a spread at a time, and past the last page the reader reacts to the episode and is offered the next one. The viewer is the package published on npm, so the paging, the spread, and the direction are the library's behaviour.

search.title: Search
search.caption: One keyword answered by the series, the authors, and the labels that match it, each group opening into a list of its own. Only what the tenant has published is searchable, so nothing still sitting in the editorial queue can be reached from here.

authors.title: Authors
authors.caption: The authors published on the tenant, with the number of series behind each name, and each author's page with a portrait, a profile, a follow, and every series credited to them. An author is a profile the editorial console manages, so one name carries across every series it is credited on.

signIn.title: Signing in
signIn.caption: An email address and a password, or the Apple and Google accounts a reader already has, on the sign-in and the sign-up form alike. The providers are the tenant's own: they appear once its console holds their credentials, and a new reader is asked to accept the tenant's terms when it names them.

account.title: A reader's own pages
account.caption: What is new from the series and authors the reader follows, the episodes they bought with how long each stays readable, and how they want to be told about a new episode — by mail, or by a notification from the browser.

dashboard.title: Dashboard
dashboard.caption: Published series, draft episodes, and scheduled releases, above the queue of everything still needing attention. The queue gathers the drafts and the upcoming releases with when each goes out, so an editor opening the console is shown what is waiting rather than having to go looking for it.

series.title: Series
series.caption: Titles, labels, publication dates, reading period, age rating, and status in one table, narrowed by serialization state or by rating. A series opens into its details: a credit for every author in the role they hold and the share of sales it earns, with the publisher's remainder worked out as the shares are typed. Those credits are the template its new episodes start from.

episodes.title: Episodes
episodes.caption: Every episode of a series in reading order, dragged into place — or moved with an arrow key — rather than renumbered by hand. An episode is scheduled for a time in the tenant's own zone, and its pages go up as images, a ZIP, or an EPUB, then are reordered the same way.

authors.title: Authors
authors.caption: The roles this tenant credits authors in, renamed and moved into the priority the credits follow, and each author's own page. A tenant admin links the reader accounts that belong to an author there, so the author reads their own episodes without buying them and is not asked to rate them.

payments.title: Payments
payments.caption: The provider this tenant's web checkout runs through — Stripe or PAY.JP — with its keys, and the App Store and Google Play credentials its app sells through. A secret is write-only: coming back, an editor sees its state and a mask, never the value.

signIn.title: Sign-in and app links
signIn.caption: The Apple and Google accounts this tenant's readers can sign in with, and the Android and iOS apps its links open in. Both are per tenant, so every publisher on one install signs its readers in under its own name and hands its links to its own app.

theme.title: Theme
theme.caption: The brand colors, the text drawn on each of them, and the typefaces readers see first, beside the logo and the icon the public site carries, with a preview built from the parts the public site is made of. The preview follows every edit while the public site keeps its current colors, so nothing reaches readers until the theme is saved.

site.title: Pages and announcements
site.caption: The tenant's own pages written in Markdown, with a translation per language and every published version kept to compare and roll back to, and the announcements it delivers to everyone who opens the site — one of them pinned as a banner across the top of every page.

contact.title: Contact messages
contact.caption: What readers sent through the site's contact form, with the address to answer at and whether anyone has dealt with it yet. A new message is mailed to the staff as well, so nobody has to keep the console open to hear about it.

reports.title: Reports and royalties
reports.caption: How many members finish each episode, and a month's sales, refunds, and what each author is owed, cut at the month's edges in the tenant's own time zone. Closing the month turns it into a statement that no later sale changes and that downloads as CSV.

auditLog.title: Audit log
auditLog.caption: Who did what, when, and how it turned out, with the actor and the record each action touched. It filters by period, action, or actor, and the dates are read as calendar days in the tenant's own time zone rather than the server's.

dashboard.title: Dashboard
dashboard.caption: What the install still needs set up, with a way into each setting, above the count of tenants and the recent cross-tenant events — tenants created, roles granted, accounts added. An operator opening the console sees whether the install is ready before anything else.

tenants.title: Tenants
tenants.caption: Every registered tenant with its status and the day it was created, searchable by name or ID, and each one's profile, domains, and members. This console manages a tenant's status and who administers it, and stays out of the catalog, which each tenant runs from its own console.

users.title: Users
users.caption: The readers of every tenant in one list, with the tenant they belong to, the day they registered, and their status. This is where an operator suspends or removes an account, while what those readers may read stays with the tenant that published it.

settings.title: Install settings
settings.caption: The one S3-compatible bucket every tenant's uploads go to, the SMTP relay the install sends through, the limits that guard sign-in and mail, and the key pair Web Push signs with. A saved change reaches every running server without a restart.

catalog.title: Catalog
catalog.caption: The tenant's name and theme in the app bar, the announcement the console pinned, and the episode the reader stopped at, above the genres and the week's chart. A bar along the bottom reaches home, search, the library, notifications, and the account from every screen but the viewer.

browse.title: Genres and search
browse.caption: The genres drawn as tiles of their covers, each opening into its series with the same sorting and filters the site offers, and one keyword answered by the series, the authors, and the labels that match it. Every list is answered by the same public API the site reads, so only what the tenant has published can be found.

seriesDetail.title: Series and authors
seriesDetail.caption: Cover, credits in the roles the tenant defined, label, genres, and tags, with a follow for the series and for each author and Share handing out the site's own link. An author's page carries the same follow, and a new episode from someone the reader follows arrives as a push notification that opens straight into the viewer.

viewer.title: Episode viewer
viewer.caption: The episode the site serves, laid out from the spread and the reading direction the editor set on it, with a slider that moves through the pages. A paid episode is bought in the store's own sheet or through the site's checkout, whichever the tenant chose, and a screenshot of a page is met with the tenant's notice on how its pages may be used.

library.title: Library and inbox
library.caption: Continue reading, follows, and the episodes saved on the device, each a list of its own; the episodes the reader bought with how long each stays readable; and the inbox of what was sent to them. Saved pages are kept encrypted under a key the device mints for itself, and reading done offline is sent once the network returns.

account.title: Account
account.caption: Everything a reader does with their account without leaving the app — the name, the address, the password, the linked Apple and Google accounts, a message to the tenant, and deleting the account — and a sign-in that offers Google on Android and Apple on iOS beside an email address.

verification.title: Confirming an address
verification.caption: The first mail a new reader receives: the button that confirms the address, when the link expires, and the link written out for a client that shows no buttons.

passwordReset.title: Resetting a password
passwordReset.caption: The link that sets a new password, expiring a day after it was sent, in the same layout the tenant's other mail uses.

contactMessage.title: A message for staff
contactMessage.caption: What a reader sent through the contact form, with the address to answer at and the account they were signed in as, so staff can reply from their own mail client.

architecture.title: How the pieces fit together
architecture.lead: Next.js at the front, one Go server behind Connect RPC with a worker beside it, and nothing underneath that you cannot already run.
architecture.processes: One publira server process carries the public, admin, and platform namespaces and delivers the images for both the reader’s origin and the console’s. publira worker, from the same binary, delivers the mail and the push notifications and runs every scheduled job: promoting due episodes, applying the free-window boundaries, turning over each tenant’s calendar day, rebuilding the charts, closing royalty months, and purging what has outlived its retention. Running it is all the scheduling a deployment needs. An optional email-renderer draws the HTML part of each mail, and publiractl migrates the database, creates its roles, sets an install up, and runs any of the worker’s jobs by hand.
architecture.tracing: Every layer is instrumented with OpenTelemetry, so one browser request reads as a single trace: the Next.js root span, the Connect RPC it makes during SSR, the identically named span on the Go side, and the db.query children below it. Point it at whatever collector you already run, or leave tracing off — it is disabled by default.

requirements.title: What it needs to run
requirements.lead: Ordinary infrastructure with no managed service behind it — bring your own, or keep the ones the Compose file brings up for you.

proxy.name: A reverse proxy
proxy.purpose: Routes each tenant's hosts to its site and console, and /api and /images to the server. The repository ships configurations for Traefik, nginx, and Caddy.

postgres.name: PostgreSQL
postgres.purpose: The catalog, tenants, users, purchases, and the audit log. Each server connects as its own role.

cache.name: A Redis-compatible cache
cache.purpose: The shared Next.js cache, so a deployment can run more than one instance behind a load balancer.

storage.name: S3-compatible object storage
storage.purpose: Episode pages, eye-catches, and the other uploads. The bucket is saved with the install's settings rather than in each process's environment.

smtp.name: An SMTP relay
smtp.purpose: Account mail, notifications, and the notices staff receive, configured per platform and per tenant.

payments.name: A payment provider
payments.purpose: One account per tenant, for paid episodes only: Stripe or PAY.JP on the web, and the App Store and Google Play in the app. A signed notification from the provider is what confirms a purchase.

firebase.name: A Firebase project
firebase.purpose: One per tenant app. Push notifications to the mobile app, sent through Firebase Cloud Messaging, which relays to APNs for iOS.

openTelemetry.name: An OpenTelemetry collector
openTelemetry.purpose: Traces from the Next.js apps and the Go servers; off unless enabled.

libraries.title: Two pieces you can take on their own
libraries.lead: Both are Apache-2.0, both are used by Publira in production paths, and neither asks you to adopt the platform to use it.

comicViewer.tagline: The React comic viewer that renders the episode screen, extracted so the UI and the data pipeline stay entirely yours.

points.headless: Headless UI architecture — compose independent, tree-shakeable components and style every one of them yourself.
points.spreads: Responsive spreads that switch between single and double pages as the container width changes.
points.virtualization: Virtualization that holds large volumes of high-resolution pages without crashing a mobile browser.
points.plugins: A pluggable data pipeline: inject fetching, decryption, or analytics through definePlugin().
points.direction: Right-to-left by default for manga, left-to-right for Western comics, with swipe, click, and keyboard navigation built in.
points.resolvePage: Lazy page metadata through resolvePage(), for long documents and expiring signed URLs.

comicViewer.note: Pre-1.0: within a 0.x line, patch releases aim to preserve compatibility, while a minor release may change the public API. Read the changelog before upgrading.

epub.tagline: A Go library for decoding, encoding, and validating EPUB 3, built for servers that never see a file on disk.

points.filesystem: Filesystem-independent: Decode takes an io.ReaderAt plus the archive size, and nothing else.
points.failFast: Fail-fast — a structural violation comes back as a DecodeError immediately.
points.memory: Memory efficient, with on-demand stream access through Asset.Open.
points.naming: Strict validation of EBPAJ and KADOKAWA-style naming and directory rules.
points.fixedLayout: Fixed-layout image pages wrapped in SVG, so page-fit survives the reading system.
points.landmarks: Structural semantics for cover, table of contents, bodymatter, index, and glossary landmarks.

epub.note: Generated publications can be checked against the official W3C EPUBCheck through the script the repository ships, which caches the tool under .tools/.

start.title: Running an install
start.lead: An install runs from container images and one Compose file, and publiractl brings its database and its first tenant into service. The host needs Docker and nothing else.
start.build: No registry publishes the images yet, so an install builds the ones it runs from a checkout of the release it wants, with the repository root as the build context. The email renderer and the platform console are optional and are built the same way when the install runs them.
start.secrets: infra/deploy/.env.example lists every value the Compose file reads; copied to .env, a required one left empty stops docker compose before anything starts. PUBLIRA_AUTH_JWT_SECRET signs the access tokens the server verifies, each web app seals its session cookie with a key of its own, and PUBLIRA_SECRET_ENCRYPTION_KEYS seals the stored credentials — the SMTP password, the object store's key, and each tenant's payment and push keys.
start.service: The first two commands apply the migrations and create the roles each process connects as, with the passwords from .env. publiractl setup then asks for the object store, the SMTP relay, the tenant, and its first administrator, and prints the addresses of the tenant site and its console. On every later release, pull or build the new images and run db migrate and db roles before docker compose up -d.
start.status: What the repository ships today is a Compose file for a single host and the images it runs, built from source. The schema, the APIs, and the surfaces above are still moving and nothing here has been through a stable release, so an install follows changes that are still landing. Issues and pull requests are the fastest way to shape where it goes next.
